newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - Dec 20.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - Dec 20.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

The Industry Commission has alarmed the automotive industry by recommending tariffs on cars and car parts be reduced from 15 per cent to five per cent by 2004. The cuts recommended are to be 2.5 per cent per year until 2000 with a five per cent cut in 201 thought to bring immediate benefits. Page 1.

An OECD report has warned Australia that it may need to make further Budget cuts in order to meet its medium-term fiscal target. The report also predicts a growth rate of 3.3 per cent for the year ahead and a need for greater recognition in the Budget of the strain of an ageing population on structural balance. Page 1.

The Federal Government has argued against the ACTU's "living wage" by saying its case for the existence of "wage poverty" is flawed as it fails to acknowledge tax transfers which boost the income of low-wage earners. The Government also said the ACTU's claim would increase unemployment. Page 3.

A week after its inception, the START grant funding program has allocated A$23.4 million to five research and development projects. The grants went to World Geoscience Corp (A$9 million), Intec Copper (A$6.4 million), Cutting Edge Technology (A$5 million, Cortecs Australia (A$2.2 million and Quantum Technology (A$0.9 million). Page 3.
THE AUSTRALIAN

The Federal Government has come under increasing pressure to speed up the reform of tariffs, taxes and industrial relations in an effort to improve the economy. In a major report, the Productivity Commission has urged the Government to agree to widespreadtariff cuts, implement a goods and services tax and has warned that the industrial relations reforms that have already been approved in the Senate did not go far enough. Page 1.

The Federal Government has initiated a strategy aiming to combat business criticism that it lacks vision and direction. A special Cabinet meeting yesterday expressed concern that leading business figures had attacked the Government's performance, despite key election promises being implemented. Pressure on the Government intensified yesterday when Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett backed News Corporation chief Rupert Murdoch's criticisms. Page 1.

Australians have broken the stereotype, according to the latest national health survey which reveals that we're seeing doctors regularly, taking vitamins, exercising and passing over cigarettes and alcohol. Over 35 per cent of Australians say their health is very good and 20 per cent claim their health is excellent. However, long-term aliments such as asthma, and high blood pressure have also increased. Page 1.

Queensland prison officers have come under scrutiny after an inquiry found up to 60 per cent of the State's inmates used drugs and procedures aimed at stopping the trade were "severely wanting". The inquiry also found that the involvement of prison offices and other staff in the drug problem was greater than expected and a Proactive Intelligence group has been recommended to combat drug trafficking in prisons. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

The Federal Government's forecasts of an improving outlook for unemployment and foreign debt have been questioned by an Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) report. The international economic forecasting body says an economic slowdown over the next two years will impact on unemployment and foreign debt and Australia has also been warned of the risk of renewed inflationary pressure - particularly if wages grow too fast. Page 1.

The New South Wales Government has reversed its pledge to confine the sale of the A$10,000 Olympic Gold passes to individuals after the Olympic stadium's backers threatened to scrap the deal. Following poor sales, underwriters demanded to be allowed to sell the passes to companies. Additional proposals being considered by the Government include approval to allow the packages to be sold internationally. Less than half of the 34,000 gold passes have been sold. Page 1.

The New South Wales workers' compensation scheme will post a A$454 million deficit for this year which has led the Carr Government to slash lump-sum compensation payouts. The WorkCover Authority's annual report to be tabled in Parliament today, will outline that the scheme has fallen from a A$57 million-plus surplus last year to a point where resources are stretched. The New South Wales Government will look at initiating a legislative overhaul to ensure the viability of the compensation scheme. Page 2.

An internal New South Wales police discussion paper has called on the Government to halve the number of police stations across the State. The confidential report also recommends that the 164 police patrols should be halved progressively. Although the conclusions of the report contradict Police Minister Whelan's claim that station closures are off the agenda, the document backs recommendations of a Government restructuring council which calls for the closure of 107 police stations. Page 3.
THE AGE

Leftist rebels in Peru have continued their hostage siege into its second day, threatening to kill 480 diplomats one by one if their demands are not met. The rebels have already let one deadline pass and released four hostages. These were the Canadian, Greek and German ambassadors and the French cultural attache to Peru. Page A1.

The Productivity Commission has stunned Victoria's car industry by recommending that local car makers have their tariffs slashed from 25 per cent to five per cent by 2004. The report also recommended the Government axe the export facilitation scheme it had just reinstated after an intense diplomatic battle with the United States. Page A1.

Sydney-Melbourne rivalry erupted again yesterday with Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett delivering a savage assessment of the New South Wales Government's record. Acting New South Wales Premier Andrew Refshauge returned the anger with a comment that compare Kennett to a small town sheriff who was jealous that Sydney was hosting the Olympics in 2000. Page A1.

A second autopsy of Jennifer Tanner's body has revealed she could not have committed suicide. Tanner's body was found in 1984 shot twice in the head. The new findings require another inquiry to be held with a request by the Attorney-General to quash the 1985 coroner's open finding and to order a fresh inquest. Page A3.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
